messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault occurred on a late October evening along the western fence line of Elias Rahme’s forty-acre property. Two men had approached without warning, and when one of them pinned him against the rusted gate, Elias felt his own heart begin to hammer against his ribs in a frantic, out-of-control drumming. The attacker’s face was inches from his, and Elias could smell the hot, sour tang of sweat mixing with the damp earth. When Elias tried to speak, his voice caught, the moment fracturing into disjointed flashes—a torn sleeve, a glint of a wristwatch, a voice growling threats that dissolved into static. Even now, when he tries to recount the incident to his wife or the sheriff, he reaches for the middle of the story only to lose the thread entirely, the narrative dissolving before he can finish. What frightens him most is that the memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, and when they surface, they feel like they belong to someone else rather than to him, a cold, detached recording he cannot step into. As the weeks turned to months, the farm became the setting where his body stayed locked in that original moment of panic. A sudden gust through the open barn door or the sight of a neighbor leaning against a fence post with a watchful, suspicious posture would send his pulse spiking. Whenever his own heart raced or pounded in his chest, the somatic echo of the attack returned, and the dread demanded immediate action. He could not stand to sit still when his body braced for danger, so he found himself throwing himself into work or tasks to keep his mind occupied. The scent of another farmer’s work-soaked shirt on the delivery truck would catch him off guard, mirroring the night of the assault, and the surge of panic pushed him away from the wall calendar. In the quiet hours, when his breathing finally slowed enough for the room to feel safe, the rumination began. He lay awake running through the mechanics of how to get even with the assailant, his mind rehearsing scenarios that locked him further into the past. The unbidden fragments followed him in a different register. When these disjointed pieces of the memory felt most alien, they pressed against his ribs until he could no longer bear the silence. To stop the detachment from overwhelming him, he began crossing out dates or anniversaries connected to the event, treating the marked days as dangerous territory. He was certain that confronting the timeline would unravel him, so he avoided them entirely. Because the fragmented pieces resisted explanation, he found he could not explain clearly to his wife or his mechanic what had actually transpired, losing the thread mid-sentence and turning away. Over the autumn harvest, the avoidance and overworking compounded into a relentless rhythm. His tractor became a refuge, the grinding gears drowning out the silent pieces of the past. He had come to believe that staying busy was the only way to keep the alien memories from merging with his present reality, and every time he felt his heart pound in the field or noticed sweat on a coworker’s shirt, the urge to flee the calendar and throw himself into the next task tightened like a coil. Six months after the first crossing-out on the calendar, Elias finally walked into the community health clinic. His wife had found the logbook of avoided dates beside his pillow and noticed how his hands trembled over the coffee cup. He sought help because the overworking was no longer enough to quiet the revenge rumination, and the memory of the assault had begun to bleed into his waking hours, stealing his sleep and his patience with his family. He was hoping, though he did not say it aloud, that someone could help him untangle the pieces without forcing him to relive the horror, and that he might finally lay down the weight of the scenarios he kept rehearsing.
